title: Chapter 2.  History — Ancient Roots to the Freedom Movement

blocks.content: A&N history is exam-gold chiefly because of the Cellular Jail and the Indian National Army/Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose connection — questions on the freedom-struggle chapter of A&N history appear disproportionately often relative to the territory's small population.
Ancient & Colonial Background

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Cellular Jail ('Kala Pani') was constructed by the British between 1896 and 1906 in Port Blair to subject Indian political prisoners to solitary confinement.
During World War II, Japanese forces occupied the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from March 1942 until October 1945.
Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose hoisted the Indian National Flag at Port Blair on 30th December 1943, declaring the islands as the first liberated Indian territory.
Netaji named Andaman as 'Shaheed Dweep' and Nicobar as 'Swaraj Dweep' during his historic 1943 visit.
In December 2018, three prominent islands were formally renamed to honor Netaji and the freedom struggle.

blocks.content: The indigenous Negrito and Mongoloid tribal groups of the islands are believed to have lived in near-total isolation for tens of thousands of years, making them among the oldest continuously surviving human populations in the world; genetic and anthropological studies link the Andamanese Negrito groups to some of the earliest waves of human migration out of Africa along the southern coastal route.

European contact began with sporadic visits by Marco Polo (13th century, who described the islanders unfavourably) and later European mariners, but sustained colonial presence started only in the late 18th century.

The British East India Company established the first colonial settlement in 1789 at Chatham Island near Port Blair (named after Lieutenant Archibald Blair, who surveyed the islands); this early settlement was abandoned by 1796 due to disease.

The British returned permanently after the Revolt of 1857, converting the islands into a penal settlement to transport and imprison Indian freedom fighters and mutineers ('Kala Pani' / 'Black Water' exile), formally re-establishing the settlement in 1858.

blocks.content: The Cellular Jail ('Kala Pani')
On 30th December 1943, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose hoisted the Tricolor at Port Blair, marking the Andaman and Nicobar Islands as the first Indian territory liberated from British rule.

The Cellular Jail (also called 'Kala Pani') in Port Blair is the single most tested monument of the entire UT. Built between 1896 and 1906, it was designed on the Pentonville/panopticon 'radial' model with seven wings radiating from a central watchtower, allowing warders to observe all wings from one point.

Originally the jail had 693 solitary cells across seven wings/spokes, each cell measuring about 13.5 ft × 7.5 ft, deliberately designed with no possibility of communication between prisoners — hence 'Cellular'. Only three wings survive today after damage during WWII Japanese occupation and later demolitions; the surviving structure is a National Memorial.

It housed political prisoners under brutal conditions — forced coconut-husk/oil-mill labour, flogging, solitary confinement, and poor food. The most iconic prisoner was Vinayak Damodar (Veer) Savarkar, who was imprisoned here from 1911, sentenced to two consecutive transportation-for-life terms (effectively 50 years).
Other notable prisoners included Batukeshwar Dutt, Yogendra Shukla, Fazl-e-Haq Khairabadi, Sohan Singh Josh, and members of the Ghadar Party, Wahhabi movement, and Bengal revolutionary groups.
A Light and Sound Show is held at the Cellular Jail every evening, and the site was declared a National Memorial in 1979 by then Prime Minister Morarji Desai.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Cellular Jail facts most commonly tested: 7 wings (radial/panopticon design), 693 total cells, built 1896–1906, only 3 wings survive, Savarkar imprisoned from 1911 with two life terms (50 years total), declared National Memorial in 1979.
Freedom Movement, Japanese Occupation & Netaji's Andaman Connection
During World War II, Japan occupied the Andaman & Nicobar Islands from March 1942 to October 1945 — the only Indian territory under Japanese occupation during the war.

Subhas Chandra Bose, leader of the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) and head of the Azad Hind Government (Provisional Government of Free India), visited Port Blair on 29–30 December 1943. On this visit he hoisted the Indian tricolour for the first time on Indian soil at the Gymkhana Ground (now Netaji Stadium), and symbolically renamed the Andaman Islands 'Shaheed Dweep' (Martyr Island) and the Nicobar Islands 'Swaraj Dweep' (Self-Rule Island).

Despite this symbolic 'liberation', the Japanese occupation itself was marked by severe repression, including espionage crackdowns and the execution of many local residents suspected of spying for the British (notably around the 'Homfreyganj Martyrs' massacre).

After Independence, the Government of India officially renamed Ross Island as 'Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep' and Neil Island and Havelock Island as 'Shaheed Dweep' and 'Swaraj Dweep' respectively in 2018, honouring Netaji's 1943 visit and the martyrs of the freedom struggle.

cells: Netaji's 1943 symbolic renaming of Nicobar as 'Swaraj Dweep'
Netaji's 1943 symbolic renaming of Andaman as 'Shaheed Dweep'

items: Cellular Jail Architecture: Designed with 7 spokes radiating from a central watchtower, containing exactly 693 individual cells to ensure total isolation.
Netaji's Naming Convention: Netaji originally designated Andaman as 'Shaheed' (Martyr) and Nicobar as 'Swaraj' (Self-rule) in 1943.
2018 Island Renamings: Ross Island became Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Dweep, Havelock Island became Swaraj Dweep, and Neil Island became Shaheed Dweep.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: PM Narendra Modi formally renamed these three islands on 30 December 2018, the 75th anniversary of Netaji hoisting the flag in Port Blair (29–30 Dec 1943) — a very frequently asked current-affairs-cum-history date.
Post-Independence & Recent Renamings

items: A&N Islands became a Union Territory of India upon Independence in 1947 and were formally recognised as a UT under the Constitution.
In 2020–21, the Government of India renamed 21 unnamed islands of the Andaman & Nicobar chain after Param Vir Chakra awardees, to honour India's highest gallantry award recipients.

In September 2024, the Government renamed the strategically important Great Nicobar's proposed development-related landmark and also announced the 'Great Nicobar Island Development Project' — a major infrastructure and strategic initiative (covered in the Economy/Schemes chapters).

blocks.content: Quick Revision Points

items: First British settlement: 1789 at Chatham Island (Lt. Archibald Blair); penal settlement re-established 1858 after 1857 Revolt.
Cellular Jail: built 1896–1906, radial 7-wing design, 693 cells, only 3 wings survive; National Memorial since 1979.
Veer Savarkar imprisoned in Cellular Jail from 1911, two consecutive life terms.
Japanese occupation: March 1942 – October 1945, the only Indian territory occupied by Japan in WWII.
Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose hoisted the Tricolour at Port Blair on 30 December 1943, renaming Andaman 'Shaheed Dweep' and Nicobar 'Swaraj Dweep'.
2018: Ross Island → Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep; Neil Island → Shaheed Dweep; Havelock Island → Swaraj Dweep.
21 unnamed islands renamed after Param Vir Chakra awardees (2020–21).
